paras: The lynching of Banjo Peavy took place at Fort Valley, Georgia, on the night of June 8, 1903, when a crowd of armed men took Peavy, a Black man, from a sheriff's guard and hanged and shot him for the killing of W. Cope Winslow Jr. earlier that day. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story nationally, a coroner's jury found that Peavy died at the hands of "unknown parties," and Black papers noted it only in briefs and lynching lists.

Winslow, 23, was the son of a man described as a leading member of the Georgia bar and the main support of his widowed mother and three sisters. Peavy reportedly owed him a small sum, and Winslow had asked him to work off the debt on his farm.

The shooting took place about 2 p.m. on June 8, some two and a half miles from Fort Valley. In the Associated Press version, Peavy "refused impudently" and shot Winslow through the forehead, and Winslow fired twice at him as he fled. The Atlanta Constitution's Fort Valley correspondent wrote that only one or two other Black men were present, and that the one who brought the news to town said Winslow also had a pistol.

A posse captured Peavy in nearby woods and turned him over to Sheriff Cooper, who had come from Perry, the county seat, to which Peavy was awaiting transport. About 8:30 p.m. a large armed crowd overpowered the specially deputized guards, who according to the Savannah Morning News made "no determined resistance." Peavy was hanged at Branham's Grove, within the town limits, and about 300 bullets were fired into his body.

Winslow's funeral the next day was largely attended, and excitement still ran high. At the inquest, many subpoenaed witnesses gave no information on who took part, and the jury found death from pistol-shot wounds by unknown parties. No report of arrests or indictments appears in the coverage. On July 6 the Birmingham Age-Herald argued that Governor Terrell could stop lynching by having the ringleaders of "the lynching bee at Fort Valley" indicted, and accused him of "winking one eye at the lynchers."

The Macon dispatch ran on June 9 and 10 from Savannah to Wichita, Salt Lake City, New Haven and Washington. Headlines cast the lynching as retribution: "Lynched His Slayer" in Savannah, "Swift Vengeance by Judge Lynch" in the Raleigh News & Observer and "Negro Hanged After Killing His Master" in the New Haven Journal and Courier. One-line digests in Minneapolis, Wisconsin and Louisiana papers placed the hanging "at Macon," the dateline.

The Americus Times-Recorder, which knew Winslow's family, headed its story "A Brutal Crime Is Avenged," called the dead man a "black brute" and said the crowd "knew the laws delay and how so often justice is defeated." The Alexandria Gazette called the shooting "a most atrocious murder" and the lynchers "a hastily-formed mob," and the Age-Herald editorial was the only item found that pressed for prosecution.

No Black newspaper in the coverage printed its own account or an editorial. The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate and the St. Louis Palladium ran the wire brief, misspelling the dead man as "Cope Wainslaw." The Indianapolis Freeman listed "'Banjo' Peavey, colored, Fort Valley, Ga." among June's lynchings, the Seattle Republican repeated the list, and the Chicago Broad Ax's year-end chronology gave the charge as "murder of W. C. Winslow."

The Times-Recorder first named the lynched man Sandy Williams but called him Banjo Peavy the next day. Its version had the man defy an unarmed Winslow earlier, return armed, and fire after Winslow fired twice and missed, followed by an eight-hour chase over fifteen miles. It put the hanging at a livery stable, while the Constitution said the crowd marched toward the Marshallville road. The Savannah inquest note dated the lynching to a Tuesday, against the dispatches' June 8.

reader.title: Lynching of Banjo Peavy
bases: A crowd of armed men took Peavy from a sheriff's specially deputized guard at Fort Valley and hanged and shot him for the killing of W. Cope Winslow Jr. (A4, A28, A7).

Peavy was taken from officers by 'a large crowd of armed citizens', hanged and riddled with bullets, and a coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties (A28, A4, A20); the act was framed as avenging the killing of Winslow, for which the papers said 'the laws delay' would defeat justice (A4, A7).

The Associated Press dispatch from Macon (A4, A2), an independent Fort Valley special to the Atlanta Constitution (A28) and the Americus Times-Recorder's own account (A7) agree that the man accused of killing Winslow was taken from custody and lynched the same night, and a coroner's inquest followed (A20).

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Macon
accounts.gist: Peavy, asked to work off a small debt, 'refused impudently' and shot Winslow through the forehead; Winslow fired twice at him as he fled; a posse soon captured him; at 8:30 p.m. the officer and guard were overpowered and he was hanged in a grove in town and shot about 300 times.

accounts.label: Fort Valley special to the Atlanta Constitution, relaying a Black eyewitness
accounts.gist: Only one or two Black men saw the shooting; one told the town that Winslow also had a pistol and shot at Peavy twice as he ran; Peavy was caught in nearby woods, handed to Sheriff Cooper, and taken by a large armed crowd from deputized guards.

accounts.label: Americus Times-Recorder
accounts.gist: The man, named 'Sandy Williams', had defied an unarmed Winslow earlier, returned armed, and fired after Winslow fired twice and missed; he was chased eight hours over fifteen miles and lynched at a livery stable before hundreds.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death from pistol-shot wounds by unknown parties; no witness identified any participant.

accounts.label: Black-press wire items and lists
accounts.gist: Cope 'Wainslaw' was murdered by a Negro at Fort Valley and the Negro was lynched; later listed among June lynchings.

framing.detail: The Americus Times-Recorder headlined 'A Brutal Crime Is Avenged', called Peavy a 'black brute' and 'Black Fiend', and explained the mob's distrust of 'the laws delay'.

AP reprints under headlines such as 'Lynched His Slayer' (Savannah), 'Negro Murderer Lynched' (Deseret) and 'Negro Hanged After Killing His Master' (New Haven), with the line that 'older and wiser citizens' deplored it.
The Alexandria Gazette called the shooting 'a most atrocious murder' and the lynchers 'a hastily-formed mob'.
The Birmingham Age-Herald's 'Going Too Far' blamed Governor Terrell for 'winking one eye at the lynchers' and urged indictment of the Fort Valley ringleaders.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate and St. Louis Palladium ran the wire brief without comment, and the Freeman, Seattle Republican and Broad Ax entered the case in lynching lists.

info: Winslow was shot about 2 p.m. (Americus: just after noon) on June 8, 1903; Peavy was lynched about 8:30 p.m. the same day

Shooting about 2.5 miles from Fort Valley, near a farm owned by Winslow's mother; lynching within Fort Valley's corporate limits at Branham's Grove (AP), at a livery stable/'pole in heart of city' (Americus), or toward the Marshallville road (Constitution)
Banjo Peavy (also 'Peavey', 'Beavy'), described as a 'negro'; the Americus Times-Recorder first named him Sandy Williams, then Banjo Peavy
Accused of shooting and killing W. Cope Winslow Jr. in a dispute over a small debt Winslow asked him to work off
A crowd of armed 'citizens' of Fort Valley; none identified; inquest verdict 'unknown parties'
